alarm: High access (arterial) pressure alarm: very negative
localises: Inflow problem: the pump can't pull blood in fast enough.
differential: Hypovolaemia / inadequate circulating volume
Catheter malposition or kinking
Patient position occluding the access lumen (common with femoral lines on hip flexion)
Access lumen thrombus
firstActions: Check and reposition the patient / limb
Flush or aspirate the access lumen to check patency
Reassess volume status
Consider reducing Qb temporarily if access-limited

localises: Outflow obstruction: resistance to blood returning to the patient.
differential: Kink in the venous (return) limb of the circuit
Clot in the venous limb or drip/deaeration chamber
Return catheter lumen malposition or thrombus
Patient position
firstActions: Inspect the full return limb for kinks
Check the deaeration chamber for clot
Flush/aspirate the return lumen if accessible
Reposition patient/catheter

localises: Membrane clotting or fouling: the machine is working harder to push fluid across the membrane.
differential: Progressive filter clotting (often with high filtration fraction as the upstream driver)
Protein/lipid fouling of the membrane over time
Inadequate anticoagulation for this patient/circuit
firstActions: Check filtration fraction: reduce post-filter replacement rate or shift replacement pre-filter
Increase blood flow if access allows
Reassess anticoagulation adequacy (post-filter iCa if citrate; aPTT if heparin)
Anticipate filter change if TMP continues to climb toward the machine's ceiling

alarm: Rising pressure drop across the filter (filter pressure minus return pressure widening)
localises: Clot forming within the fibre bundle itself, distinct from a TMP rise driven by fouling.
differential: Fibre bundle clotting
Under-anticoagulation for this circuit
firstActions: Same anticoagulation reassessment as rising TMP
Prepare for filter change: a widening pressure drop with rising TMP together predict imminent clotting

localises: Air has entered the circuit, most commonly pre-pump on the access side (a loose connection or an empty priming bag) or via a cracked line.
differential: Loose or disconnected line connection
Empty bag upstream of the pump generating negative-pressure air entrainment
Cracked tubing or connector
firstActions: The machine will auto-clamp the return line: do not bypass this
Inspect all connections systematically from access to return
Do not resume until the air source is found and cleared

pressurePattern.TMP: may be elevated preceding the leak

localises: Membrane rupture: blood cells crossing into the effluent.
differential: Membrane fibre rupture, often after a period of high TMP
False positive from haemolysis or pigmenturia
firstActions: Do not ignore or override: a true leak requires the circuit to be changed
Inspect effluent visually for blood tinge
If confirmed, change the circuit; the blood in the extracorporeal circuit is not returned

alarm: No alarm: delivered dose is lower than expected despite an unremarkable-looking prescription
localises: Return blood is being pulled back into the access lumen instead of reaching systemic circulation; it is silent, and no alarm fires.
differential: Short or malpositioned catheter (classically a short femoral line)
Catheter tip abutting a vessel wall
Access and return lumens too close together for the catheter's design
firstActions: Suspect this when labs don't track with the prescribed dose despite a technically normal-looking circuit
Consider catheter reposition or exchange for a longer/better-positioned line
This is why the guided builder emphasises catheter length and site (see Learn → step 3)

alarm: Not an alarm: a planning concept
localises: Circuit downtime (filter changes, transport, line issues) reduces delivered dose even when nothing is technically wrong.
differential: Three 40-minute circuit changes in a day ≈ 120 minutes ≈ 8.3% of the day
A 25 mL/kg/hr prescription at 91.7% uptime delivers roughly 23 mL/kg/hr, before any other loss
firstActions: Prescribe above target (25–30 mL/kg/hr) to absorb expected downtime and still land at 20–25 delivered
Track uptime, not just the prescribed number, when reviewing whether dose targets are being met
